title: Diwali Airfares Surge up to 340% on Some Regional Routes
excerpt: One-way economy fares on select festive routes, from Kolkata-Deoghar to Delhi-Patna, have risen two to three times their usual levels as the Durga Puja and Diwali travel rush meets limited seat availability.
body:
• Kolkata–Deoghar fares have climbed roughly 340% — from a usual ₹2,800 to ₹12,500 — during the Durga Puja travel window, the steepest jump recorded this festive season.
  • Delhi–Patna peak-festive fares have crossed ₹12,500 against a normal ₹3,500–4,500, with last-minute direct tickets pushing past ₹13,500.
  • The sharpest spikes are on metro-to-regional routes with limited competition; major trunk routes such as Delhi–Mumbai show only moderate increases.
  • Airlines attribute the surge to record festive demand and rising fuel costs, and travellers are being urged to book well in advance.

Festive-season airfares in India have soared, with one-way economy tickets on select routes costing up to three times their usual price — and as much as 340% more on a few regional sectors. With seats on peak festive dates filling fast, airlines are selling the remaining inventory at the top of their fare buckets, leaving travellers heading home for Durga Puja, Diwali and Chhath facing unusually steep bills.

Regional routes see the sharpest spikes

The steepest increases are on sectors with limited direct-flight competition, according to fare data reported by Moneycontrol and travel portals. Kolkata–Deoghar fares, which normally cost around ₹2,800, have climbed to approximately ₹12,500 during the Durga Puja period — a jump of about 340%. Delhi–Agatti tickets have risen from a usual ₹8,500 to around ₹25,000 for peak October holiday dates, an increase of nearly 194%.

The Delhi–Patna route, one of the busiest festive corridors, shows non-stop economy fares that typically cost ₹3,500 to ₹4,500 crossing ₹12,500 on peak dates, with last-minute direct fares beyond ₹13,500. Patna Press data for early November shows Delhi–Patna tickets at ₹8,391 to ₹9,546 against a usual fare of around ₹5,500, and Delhi–Darbhanga touching ₹13,601 on November 7 against a normal ₹5,700 — more than double. Bengaluru–Jharsuguda tickets have risen from ₹4,200 to ₹16,200, roughly 285% more, while Mumbai–Bareilly fares are up from ₹4,500 to over ₹15,000.

On major metro routes the rise is comparatively moderate. Delhi–Kolkata fares have crossed ₹12,300 from an off-peak level of around ₹4,800, Delhi–Bengaluru tickets are at roughly ₹10,000, and Delhi–Mumbai is hovering around ₹7,000. Mumbai–Kolkata direct economy tickets, normally ₹5,000 to ₹6,500, are selling for ₹11,500 to ₹14,200 through the main Durga Puja travel period.

Context and background

The festive window from Dussehra through Chhath is India's peak domestic travel period, driven by millions of migrant workers, students and families returning to their hometowns. Confirmed train tickets become increasingly hard to secure as the dates approach, pushing more travellers toward flights — exactly when seat availability tightens.

Fleet delivery delays, engine maintenance and higher operating costs have also squeezed airline capacity, according to industry reporting. Fuel costs are adding to the pressure: domestic Aviation Turbine Fuel prices rose 5.46%, or ₹6.28 per litre, to ₹121.28 per litre on September 1 — the second consecutive monthly increase. Fuel accounts for 35% to 40% of airline operating costs, making it a significant input into ticket pricing.

Impact and analysis

The pricing pattern this year underlines how India's fare surge is concentrated, not uniform. Trunk routes between metros, where multiple airlines compete on frequent schedules, are seeing high but manageable increases. The pain is sharpest on regional connections — Deoghar, Agatti, Jharsuguda, Darbhanga — where a handful of carriers set the price and festive demand has nowhere else to go.

For travellers, the arithmetic is unforgiving. Low-fare buckets on high-demand sectors are being filled weeks in advance, so anyone booking late pays the residual fare — which, as the Delhi–Patna and Kolkata–Deoghar numbers show, can be three to four times the normal price. Bus and train alternatives offer little relief: inter-state bus fares have also surged, and trains remain near capacity.

Diaspora angle

For Indian-origin travellers overseas planning trips home around the festivals, the domestic-leg cost deserves a second look when budgeting. International tickets into Delhi, Mumbai or Kolkata are only half the journey for those heading onward to tier-2 and tier-3 cities — and it is precisely those onward legs where fares have multiplied. Booking domestic sectors early, or aligning travel with midweek dates rather than the festival eve, can make a material difference.

What's next

Fares typically ease once the festive rush subsides, but the pressure is unlikely to lift before Chhath, when the final wave of homeward travel completes. Aviation analysts expect last-minute fares to remain steep through the window. Travellers who have not yet booked are advised to lock in tickets now rather than gamble on late availability, and to check alternate dates — fares on the actual day of a festival are often lower than on the days immediately before it.
